summary:
AstroVitals AI is a bilingual prototype for monitoring astronaut health during space missions. It displays six vital signs and compares simulated readings with personalized baselines, taking activity and mission context into account. Interactive scenarios show how changes across multiple indicators can trigger alerts, while charts, space-health information, and a crew-response checklist help users understand what changed and what steps may follow.
The project addresses the challenge by making health information easier for astronauts to review and interpret onboard, particularly when communication with Earth may be delayed. Its goal is to support awareness and structured crew response—not replace medical professionals. The prototype currently uses synthetic demonstration data; it is not connected to live wearable sensors or a NASA health dataset, and its alert thresholds are not medically validated.
details:
On long-duration space missions such as NASA’s Artemis lunar program and future Mars expeditions, astronauts face severe physiological and environmental hazards—including space radiation, isolation, microgravity-induced cephalic fluid shifts, 10–15% plasma volume loss, cardiac deconditioning, 0.5–1°C core temperature elevation during exertion, and 1% monthly bone mineral density loss—without access to an onboard hospital. While Low Earth Orbit (ISS) crews have near-continuous contact with Ground Flight Surgeons and emergency return options within hours, lunar missions experience signal delays and multi-day return windows, and Mars missions face 3-to-22-minute one-way communication delays where emergency Earth return is practically impossible for months.

AstroVitals AI empowers astronauts and Crew Medical Officers (CMOs) to detect health anomalies early, understand physiological changes in microgravity, and execute step-by-step medical countermeasures autonomously before minor deviations escalate into life-threatening emergencies.

How AstroVitals AI Works (Key Features)

1. Activity-Adjusted & Personalized Vital Sign Monitoring

- Tracks 6 core vital signs—Heart Rate (bpm), Systolic & Diastolic Blood Pressure (mmHg), SpO2 (%), Respiratory Rate (breaths/min), and Body Temperature (°C)—alongside ECG intervals (PR, QRS, QTc), Heart Rate Variability (HRV/RMSSD), Sleep Duration, Cabin CO2 (mmHg), and Daily Radiation Dose (mSv/day).

- Dynamically adjusts reference thresholds based on the astronaut's real-time activity: Rest/Light Activity, Sleep, or Daily Exercise (~2.5 hours/day).

- Evaluates every reading against each crew member’s Personal Baseline (Mean ± SD) using real-time Z-score calculations: triggering a Warning at |Z| ≥ 2.0 and a Critical alert at |Z| ≥ 3.0, even if a reading falls within general population ranges.

- Detects gradual deterioration via a 6-hour moving average trend rule (>10% shift over 24 hours triggers a Notice alert) and escalates compound anomalies (simultaneous elevated HR, low SpO2, and elevated respiratory rate at rest) immediately to Critical status.

2. Interactive Astronaut Anatomical Digital Twin

- Features a clickable anatomical human body interface where affected organ systems (Neurological/Sleep, Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Thermoregulation, and Musculoskeletal) dynamically change color (Green: Normal, Blue: Notice, Yellow: Warning, Red: Critical).

- Clicking anybody region educates the astronaut on its physiological function, how spaceflight differs from Earth (including fluid shift and post-flight orthostatic intolerance), and active countermeasures.

3. 5-Tier Alert Engine & 8-Step Zero-Gravity Emergency Protocol

- Implements a 5-level alert hierarchy (Normal, Notice, Warning, Critical, and Emergency with audio alarm) mapped to 14 condition-specific space medicine protocols (including Tachycardia, Bradycardia, Hypertension, Hypotension, Hypoxia, Dyspnea, Hyperthermia, High Cabin CO2 > 5.3 mmHg, Arrhythmia, Cardiac/Respiratory Arrest, Solar Particle Events, Sleep Deprivation, Psychological Stress, and Trauma/EVA Emergencies).

- Defines clear crew responsibility roles (Injured Astronaut, Nearest Crewmate/First Responder, Crew Medical Officer [CMO], Ground Flight Surgeon, Mission Control, and Mission Commander).

- Every triggered alert launches an interactive Command Modal featuring a live elapsed timer, probable physiological causes, an interactive 8-step microgravity checklist (including zero-G restraint strap procedures and wound fluid containment), and a one-click "Contact Flight Surgeon & Auto-Send Telemetry" action calibrated to ISS, Moon, or Mars communication delays.

4. Mission Simulation Lab & 24h / 30d Telemetry Analytics

- Seeded with a 4,320-record minute-by-minute 24-hour dataset across three astronaut profiles (AST-01 Cmdr. Layla, AST-02 Eng. Omar, and AST-03 Dr. Sara) plus 30-day historical trend charts and daily/weekly health summary reports.

- Includes one-click test scenarios (such as a tachycardia-hypoxia episode, gradual hyperthermia onset, cumulative sleep deprivation, and cabin CO2 spikes) to demonstrate autonomous triage and escalation workflows.

Technical Architecture & Tools Used

- Backend: Python, Django, Django REST Framework (DRF), and Classic Swagger UI for interactive JSON API testing and documentation.

- Frontend: React (Vite), Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion (for HUD telemetry animations), and Recharts (for real-time 24-hour and 30-day multi-axis health charts with threshold reference lines).

- Accessibility & Persistence: Bilingual interface supporting English (default) and Arabic (full RTL layout) with local and database state persistence.

Disclaimer & Reference Sources

Disclaimer: All astronaut profiles, vital sign datasets, thresholds, and emergency procedures in AstroVitals AI are synthetic/simulated data constructed from general space physiology principles for NASA Space Apps Challenge demonstration purposes only. They do not represent official NASA medical protocols or clinical advice; real-world medical decisions remain solely with the Crew Medical Officer and Flight Surgeon.

Space Agency Resources Referenced:

- NASA Human Research Program (HRP) — Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight & Spaceflight Risks (nasa.gov/hrp/hazards & nasa.gov/hrp/risks)

- NASA ISS Research — Wearable Technology, Bio-Monitor, and Holter Monitor Studies

- Canadian Space Agency (CSA) — Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health
